# Repository Constitution

Authoritative rules for all plugins in this repository. EARS-format hard constraints — the fence that all plugin development must stay inside. The interior (how an agent reasons, searches, and decides) is intentionally unconstrained.

All rules use EARS notation: WHEN / IF / WHERE / WHILE / THE SYSTEM SHALL.

---

## Plugin Structure

WHEN a new plugin is created, it SHALL conform to the directory layout:
```
plugins/<id>/
├── plugin.json
├── README.md
├── CHANGELOG.md
├── skills/<id>/SKILL.md
└── agents/*.md
```

A new plugin SHALL default to a single skill directory named after the plugin id. IF the plugin's scope grows to cover several genuinely independent, heterogeneous user intents on the same artifact (not a linear pipeline invoked as one flow), the plugin author MAY split `skills/<id>/` into multiple directories — `skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` per skill — each still conforming to the frontmatter and body rules below. The skill-routing key is the directory name, not the frontmatter `name:` field.

WHEN a plugin manifest (`plugin.json`) is authored, it SHALL include: `id`, `version` (semver), `description`, `skills`, and `agents` (list of file paths).

IF a plugin is superseded by another, it SHALL be deleted from the repository rather than marked deprecated.

---

## Agent Structure

WHEN an agent prompt is authored, it SHALL define five named sections in the body, in this order: `<constitution>`, `<backstory>`, `<goal>`, `<judgment>`, and `<output>`.

WHEN an agent body's `<constitution>` section is authored or amended, it SHALL be byte-for-byte identical across every agent file in the ecosystem — this is the shared static prefix the Static Prompt Prefix Invariant depends on; any per-character difference breaks prompt-cache matching for every agent, not just the one edited.

WHEN an agent uses a shared reference file during e<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="3552" />tmatter, it SHALL default to a single lifecycle-stage word.

IF a single word does not communicate what the skill acts on, the plugin author SHALL use a more specific multi-word name instead (e.g. `post-review`, not `post`).

Skill names SHALL NOT be prefixed with their own plugin id to resolve a collision with another plugin's skill name (e.g. `courier-post`) — the plugin-qualified invocation (`<plugin>:<skill>`) already disambiguates two plugins using the same bare skill name, so prefixing the name itself duplicates that and adds no clarity.

---

## Reference Files

WHEN the top-level language index file (`rust.md`, `typescript.md`) is referenced, it SHALL redirect to the appropriate split file rather than containing content directly.

---

## Documentation

WHEN a plugin is published, it SHALL include a `README.md` with: purpose, when-to-use trigger phrases, agent table with modes and tiers, pipeline diagram, output schema reference, and install instructions.

# Conventional Commits Reference

**Format:** `<type>(<scope>): <description>`

Types: `feat` `fix` `docs` `style` `refactor` `test` `chore` `perf` `ci` `build` `revert`

Breaking change: append `!` after type/scope, or add `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer.

## Rules

- Subject line: imperative mood, no period, under 72 characters
- Body (optional): explain the *why*, not the what. Do not artificially wrap lines — one paragraph per line, let the terminal/renderer soft-wrap.
- Footer: `BREAKING CHANGE: <description>`, `Fixes #123`, `Refs #456`
- Scope is optional; when used, it names the module or component

## Examples

```
feat(courier): add changeset generation skill

fix(sentinel): retry gate passes specific failure message to producer

docs(shared): add conventional-commits reference

refactor(ranger): extract language detection into recon subagent

BREAKING CHANGE: plugin ID changed from bug-hunter-rust to proof.
Update marketplace.json and skill trigger references.

feat!: rename proof to ranger

BREAKING CHANGE: plugin ID changed from proof to ranger.
Update marketplace.json and skill trigger references.
```

The body answers: why was this change needed? What problem does it solve?

Active voice, imperative mood. If a sentence keeps running, it's usually doing two jobs — split it rather than trimming words to make it fit. # Repository Constitution

Authoritative rules for all plugins in this repository. EARS-format hard constraints — the fence that all plugin development must stay inside. The interior (how an agent reasons, searches, and decides) is intentionally unconstrained.

All rules use EARS notation: WHEN / IF / WHERE / WHILE / THE SYSTEM SHALL.

---

## Plugin Structure

WHEN a new plugin is created, it SHALL conform to the directory layout:
```
plugins/<id>/
├── plugin.json
├── README.md
├── CHANGELOG.md
├── skills/<id>/SKILL.md
└── agents/*.md
```

A new plugin SHALL default to a single skill directory named after the plugin id. IF the plugin's scope grows to cover several genuinely independent, heterogeneous user intents on the same artifact (not a linear pipeline invoked as one flow), the plugin author MAY split `skills/<id>/` into multiple directories — `skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` per skill — each still conforming to the frontmatter and body rules below. The skill-routing key is the directory name, not the frontmatter `name:` field.

WHEN a plugin manifest (`plugin.json`) is authored, it SHALL include: `id`, `version` (semver), `description`, `skills`, and `agents` (list of file paths).

IF a plugin is superseded by another, it SHALL be deleted from the repository rather than marked deprecated.

---

## Agent Structure

WHEN an agent prompt is authored, it SHALL define five named sections in the body, in this order: `<constitution>`, `<backstory>`, `<goal>`, `<judgment>`, and `<output>`.

WHEN an agent body's `<constitution>` section is authored or amended, it SHALL be byte-for-byte identical across every agent file in the ecosystem — this is the shared static prefix the Static Prompt Prefix Invariant depends on; any per-character difference breaks prompt-cache matching for every agent, not just the one edited.

WHEN an agent uses a shared reference file during e<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="3552" />tmatter, it SHALL default to a single lifecycle-stage word.

IF a single word does not communicate what the skill acts on, the plugin author SHALL use a more specific multi-word name instead (e.g. `post-review`, not `post`).

Skill names SHALL NOT be prefixed with their own plugin id to resolve a collision with another plugin's skill name (e.g. `courier-post`) — the plugin-qualified invocation (`<plugin>:<skill>`) already disambiguates two plugins using the same bare skill name, so prefixing the name itself duplicates that and adds no clarity.

---

## Reference Files

WHEN language-specific reference files are authored, they SHALL be split by concern: hazards, smells, tooling — one file per concern per language.

WHEN the top-level language index file (`rust.md`, `typescript.md`) is referenced, it SHALL redirect to the appropriate split file rather than containing content directly.

---

## Documentation

WHEN a plugin is published, it SHALL include a `README.md` with: purpose, when-to-use trigger phrases, agent table with modes and tiers, pipeline diagram, output schema reference, and install instructions.

WHEN editing Markdown, THE SYSTEM SHALL keep each prose paragraph on one physical source line — Markdown prose SHALL NEVER be manually wrapped.

WHEN authoring Markdown, THE SYSTEM SHALL use a succinct, friendly, engineering-focused voice and favor scannable headings, lists, tables, diagrams, and charts over dense prose.

WHEN CONTRIBUTING.md is updated, it SHALL reflect the current authoring checklist — not the authoring conventions from a prior era.

WHEN a new agent-authoring convention is added to this constitution or to CONTRIBUTING.md's checklist — a new required section, a new required check — THE SYSTEM SHALL update `mason:scaffolder` and `mason:auditor` in the same change. A convention `mason` cannot generate or verify is documented, not enforced, and every plugin scaffolded before the update inherits the gap silently.

# Repository Constitution

Authoritative rules for all plugins in this repository. EARS-format hard constraints — the fence that all plugin development must stay inside. The interior (how an agent reasons, searches, and decides) is intentionally unconstrained.

All rules use EARS notation: WHEN / IF / WHERE / WHILE / THE SYSTEM SHALL.

---

## Plugin Structure

WHEN a new plugin is created, it SHALL conform to the directory layout:
```
plugins/<id>/
├── plugin.json
├── README.md
├── CHANGELOG.md
├── skills/<id>/SKILL.md
└── agents/*.md
```

A new plugin SHALL default to a single skill directory named after the plugin id. IF the plugin's scope grows to cover several genuinely independent, heterogeneous user intents on the same artifact (not a linear pipeline invoked as one flow), the plugin author MAY split `skills/<id>/` into multiple directories — `skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` per skill — each still conforming to the frontmatter and body rules below. The skill-routing key is the directory name, not the frontmatter `name:` field.

WHEN a plugin manifest (`plugin.json`) is authored, it SHALL include: `id`, `version` (semver), `description`, `skills`, and `agents` (list of file paths).

IF a plugin is superseded by another, it SHALL be deleted from the repository rather than marked deprecated.

---

## Agent Structure

WHEN an agent prompt is authored, it SHALL define five named sections in the body, in this order: `<constitution>`, `<backstory>`, `<goal>`, `<judgment>`, and `<output>`.

WHEN an agent body's `<constitution>` section is authored or amended, it SHALL be byte-for-byte identical across every agent file in the ecosystem — this is the shared static prefix the Static Prompt Prefix Invariant depends on; any per-character difference breaks prompt-cache matching for every agent, not just the one edited.

WHEN an agent uses a shared reference file during e<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="3552" />tmatter, it SHALL default to a single lifecycle-stage word.

---

## Reference Files

WHEN language-specific reference files are authored, they SHALL be split by concern: hazards, smells, tooling — one file per concern per language.

WHEN the top-level language index file (`rust.md`, `typescript.md`) is referenced, it SHALL redirect to the appropriate split file rather than containing content directly.

---

## Documentation

WHEN a plugin is published, it SHALL include a `README.md` with: purpose, when-to-use trigger phrases, agent table with modes and tiers, pipeline diagram, output schema reference, and install instructions.

WHEN editing Markdown, THE SYSTEM SHALL keep each prose paragraph on one physical source line — Markdown prose SHALL NEVER be manually wrapped.

Authoritative rules for all plugins in this repository. EARS-format hard constraints — the fence that all plugin development must stay inside. The interior (how an agent reasons, searches, and decides) is intentionally unconstrained.

All rules use EARS notation: WHEN / IF / WHERE / WHILE / THE SYSTEM SHALL.

├── plugin.json
├── README.md
├── CHANGELOG.md
├── skills/<id>/SKILL.md
└── agents/*.md
```

A new plugin SHALL default to a single skill directory named after the plugin id. IF the plugin's scope grows to cover several genuinely independent, heterogeneous user intents on the same artifact (not a linear pipeline invoked as one flow), the plugin author MAY split `skills/<id>/` into multiple directories — `skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` per skill — each still conforming to the frontmatter and body rules below. WHEN a plugin manifest (`plugin.json`) is authored, it SHALL include: `id`, `version` (semver), `description`, `skills`, and `agents` (list of file paths).

# Repository Constitution

Authoritative rules for all plugins in this repository. EARS-format hard constraints — the fence that all plugin development must stay inside. The interior (how an agent reasons, searches, and decides) is intentionally unconstrained.

All rules use EARS notation: WHEN / IF / WHERE / WHILE / THE SYSTEM SHALL.

---

## Plugin Structure

WHEN a new plugin is created, it SHALL conform to the directory layout:
```
plugins/<id>/
├── plugin.json
├── README.md
├── CHANGELOG.md
├── skills/<id>/SKILL.md
└── agents/*.md
```

A new plugin SHALL default to a single skill directory named after the plugin id. IF the plugin's scope grows to cover several genuinely independent, heterogeneous user intents on the same artifact (not a linear pipeline invoked as one flow), the plugin author MAY split `skills/<id>/` into multiple directories — `skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` per skill — each still conforming to the frontmatter and body rules below. The skill-routing key is the directory name, not the frontmatter `name:` field.

WHEN a plugin manifest (`plugin.json`) is authored, it SHALL include: `id`, `version` (semver), `description`, `skills`, and `agents` (list of file paths).

IF a plugin is superseded by another, it SHALL be deleted from the repository rather than marked deprecated.

---

## Agent Structure

WHEN an agent prompt is authored, it SHALL define five named sections in the body, in this order: `<constitution>`, `<backstory>`, `<goal>`, `<judgment>`, and `<output>`.

WHEN an agent body's `<constitution>` section is authored or amended, it SHALL be byte-for-byte identical across every agent file in the ecosystem — this is the shared static prefix the Static Prompt Prefix Invariant depends on; any per-character difference breaks prompt-cache matching for every agent, not just the one edited.

WHEN an agent uses a shared reference file during e<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="3552" />tmatter, it SHALL default to a single lifecycle-stage word.

IF a single word does not communicate what the skill acts on, the plugin author SHALL use a more specific multi-word name instead (e.g. `post-review`, not `post`).

Skill names SHALL NOT be prefixed with their own plugin id to resolve a collision with another plugin's skill name (e.g. `courier-post`) — the plugin-qualified invocation (`<plugin>:<skill>`) already disambiguates two plugins using the same bare skill name, so prefixing the name itself duplicates that and adds no clarity.

---

## Reference Files

WHEN language-specific reference files are authored, they SHALL be split by concern: hazards, smells, tooling — one file per concern per language.

WHEN the top-level language index file (`rust.md`, `typescript.md`) is referenced, it SHALL redirect to the appropriate split file rather than containing content directly.

---

## Documentation

WHEN a plugin is published, it SHALL include a `README.md` with: purpose, when-to-use trigger phrases, agent table with modes and tiers, pipeline diagram, output schema reference, and install instructions.

WHEN editing Markdown, THE SYSTEM SHALL keep each prose paragraph on one physical source line — Markdown prose SHALL NEVER be manually wrapped.

WHEN authoring Markdown, THE SYSTEM SHALL use a succinct, friendly, engineering-focused voice and favor scannable headings, lists, tables, diagrams, and charts over dense prose.

WHEN CONTRIBUTING.md is updated, it SHALL reflect the current authoring checklist — not the authoring conventions from a prior era.

WHEN a new agent-authoring convention is added to this constitution or to CONTRIBUTING.md's checklist — a new required section, a new required check — THE SYSTEM SHALL update `mason:scaffolder` and `mason:auditor` in the same change. A convention `mason` cannot generate or verify is documented, not enforced, and every plugin scaffolded before the update inherits the gap silently.

# Repository Constitution

Authoritative rules for all plugins in this repository. EARS-format hard constraints — the fence that all plugin development must stay inside. The interior (how an agent reasons, searches, and decides) is intentionally unconstrained.

All rules use EARS notation: WHEN / IF / WHERE / WHILE / THE SYSTEM SHALL.

---

## Plugin Structure

WHEN a new plugin is created, it SHALL conform to the directory layout:
```
plugins/<id>/
├── plugin.json
├── README.md
├── CHANGELOG.md
├── skills/<id>/SKILL.md
└── agents/*.md
```

A new plugin SHALL default to a single skill directory named after the plugin id. IF the plugin's scope grows to cover several genuinely independent, heterogeneous user intents on the same artifact (not a linear pipeline invoked as one flow), the plugin author MAY split `skills/<id>/` into multiple directories — `skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` per skill — each still conforming to the frontmatter and body rules below. The skill-routing key is the directory name, not the frontmatter `name:` field.

WHEN a plugin manifest (`plugin.json`) is authored, it SHALL include: `id`, `version` (semver), `description`, `skills`, and `agents` (list of file paths).

IF a plugin is superseded by another, it SHALL be deleted from the repository rather than marked deprecated.

---

## Agent Structure

WHEN an agent prompt is authored, it SHALL define five named sections in the body, in this order: `<constitution>`, `<backstory>`, `<goal>`, `<judgment>`, and `<output>`.

WHEN an agent body's `<constitution>` section is authored or amended, it SHALL be byte-for-byte identical across every agent file in the ecosystem — this is the shared static prefix the Static Prompt Prefix Invariant depends on; any per-character difference breaks prompt-cache matching for every agent, not just the one edited.

WHEN an agent uses a shared reference file during e<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="3552" />tmatter, it SHALL default to a single lifecycle-stage word.

IF a single word does not communicate what the skill acts on, the plugin author SHALL use a more specific multi-word name instead (e.g. `post-review`, not `post`).

Skill names SHALL NOT be prefixed with their own plugin id to resolve a collision with another plugin's skill name (e.g. `courier-post`) — the plugin-qualified invocation (`<plugin>:<skill>`) already disambiguates two plugins using the same bare skill name, so prefixing the name itself duplicates that and adds no clarity.

---

## Reference Files

WHEN language-specific reference files are authored, they SHALL be split by concern: hazards, smells, tooling — one file per concern per language.

WHEN the top-level language index file (`rust.md`, `typescript.md`) is referenced, it SHALL redirect to the appropriate split file rather than containing content directly.

---

## Documentation

WHEN a plugin is published, it SHALL include a `README.md` with: purpose, when-to-use trigger phrases, agent table with modes and tiers, pipeline diagram, output schema reference, and install instructions.

WHEN editing Markdown, THE SYSTEM SHALL keep each prose paragraph on one physical source line — Markdown prose SHALL NEVER be manually wrapped.

WHEN authoring Markdown, THE SYSTEM SHALL use a succinct, friendly, engineering-focused voice and favor scannable headings, lists, tables, diagrams, and charts over dense prose.

WHEN CONTRIBUTING.md is updated, it SHALL reflect the current authoring checklist — not the authoring conventions from a prior era.

WHEN a new agent-authoring convention is added to this constitution or to CONTRIBUTING.md's checklist — a new required section, a new required check — THE SYSTEM SHALL update `mason:scaffolder` and `mason:auditor` in the same change. A convention `mason` cannot generate or verify is documented, not enforced, and every plugin scaffolded before the update inherits the gap silently.

# Repository Constitution

Authoritative rules for all plugins in this repository. EARS-format hard constraints — the fence that all plugin development must stay inside. The interior (how an agent reasons, searches, and decides) is intentionally unconstrained.

All rules use EARS notation: WHEN / IF / WHERE / WHILE / THE SYSTEM SHALL.

---

## Plugin Structure

WHEN a new plugin is created, it SHALL conform to the directory layout:
```
plugins/<id>/
├── plugin.json
├── README.md
├── CHANGELOG.md
├── skills/<id>/SKILL.md
└── agents/*.md
```

A new plugin SHALL default to a single skill directory named after the plugin id. IF the plugin's scope grows to cover several genuinely independent, heterogeneous user intents on the same artifact (not a linear pipeline invoked as one flow), the plugin author MAY split `skills/<id>/` into multiple directories — `skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` per skill — each still conforming to the frontmatter and body rules below. The skill-routing key is the directory name, not the frontmatter `name:` field.

WHEN a plugin manifest (`plugin.json`) is authored, it SHALL include: `id`, `version` (semver), `description`, `skills`, and `agents` (list of file paths).

IF a plugin is superseded by another, it SHALL be deleted from the repository rather than marked deprecated.

---

## Agent Structure

WHEN an agent prompt is authored, it SHALL define five named sections in the body, in this order: `<constitution>`, `<backstory>`, `<goal>`, `<judgment>`, and `<output>`.

WHEN an agent body's `<constitution>` section is authored or amended, it SHALL be byte-for-byte identical across every agent file in the ecosystem — this is the shared static prefix the Static Prompt Prefix Invariant depends on; any per-character difference breaks prompt-cache matching for every agent, not just the one edited.

WHEN an agent uses a shared reference file during e<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="3552" />tmatter, it SHALL default to a single lifecycle-stage word.

IF a single word does not communicate what the skill acts on, the plugin author SHALL use a more specific multi-word name instead (e.g. `post-review`, not `post`).

Skill names SHALL NOT be prefixed with their own plugin id to resolve a collision with another plugin's skill name (e.g. `courier-post`) — the plugin-qualified invocation (`<plugin>:<skill>`) already disambiguates two plugins using the same bare skill name, so prefixing the name itself duplicates that and adds no clarity.

---

## Reference Files

WHEN language-specific reference files are authored, they SHALL be split by concern: hazards, smells, tooling — one file per concern per language.

WHEN the top-level language index file (`rust.md`, `typescript.md`) is referenced, it SHALL redirect to the appropriate split file rather than containing content directly.

---

## Documentation

WHEN a plugin is published, it SHALL include a `README.md` with: purpose, when-to-use trigger phrases, agent table with modes and tiers, pipeline diagram, output schema reference, and install instructions.

WHEN editing Markdown, THE SYSTEM SHALL keep each prose paragraph on one physical source line — Markdown prose SHALL NEVER be manually wrapped.

WHEN authoring Markdown, THE SYSTEM SHALL use a succinct, friendly, engineering-focused voice and favor scannable headings, lists, tables, diagrams, and charts over dense prose.

WHEN CONTRIBUTING.md is updated, it SHALL reflect the current authoring checklist — not the authoring conventions from a prior era.

WHEN a new agent-authoring convention is added to this constitution or to CONTRIBUTING.md's checklist — a new required section, a new required check — THE SYSTEM SHALL update `mason:scaffolder` and `mason:auditor` in the same change. A convention `mason` cannot generate or verify is documented, not enforced, and every plugin scaffolded before the update inherits the gap silently.

Authoritative rules for all plugins in this repository. EARS-format hard constraints — the fence that all plugin development must stay inside. The interior (how an agent reasons, searches, and decides) is intentionally unconstrained.

## Plugin Structure

WHEN a new plugin is created, it SHALL conform to the directory layout:
```
plugins/<id>/
├── plugin.json
├── README.md
├── CHANGELOG.md
├── skills/<id>/SKILL.md
└── agents/*.md
```

A new plugin SHALL default to a single skill directory named after the plugin id. IF the plugin's scope grows to cover several genuinely independent, heterogeneous user intents on the same artifact (not a linear pipeline invoked as one flow), the plugin author MAY split `skills/<id>/` into multiple directories — `skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` per skill — each still conforming to the frontmatter and body rules below. WHEN a plugin manifest (`plugin.json`) is authored, it SHALL include: `id`, `version` (semver), `description`, `skills`, and `agents` (list of file paths).

---

## Agent Structure

WHEN an agent body's `<constitution>` section is authored or amended, it SHALL be byte-for-byte identical across every agent file in the ecosystem — this is the shared static prefix the Static Prompt Prefix Invariant depends on; any per-character difference breaks prompt-cache matching for every agent, not just the one edited.

WHEN an agent uses a shared reference file during e<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="3552" />tmatter, it SHALL default to a single lifecycle-stage word.

---

## Documentation

WHEN a plugin is published, it SHALL include a `README.md` with: purpose, when-to-use trigger phrases, agent table with modes and tiers, pipeline diagram, output schema reference, and install instructions.

WHEN editing Markdown, THE SYSTEM SHALL keep each prose paragraph on one physical source line — Markdown prose SHALL NEVER be manually wrapped.

WHEN authoring Markdown, THE SYSTEM SHALL use a succinct, friendly, engineering-focused voice and favor scannable headings, lists, tables, diagrams, and charts over dense prose.

WHEN CONTRIBUTING.md is updated, it SHALL reflect the current authoring checklist — not the authoring conventions from a prior era.

# ADR-008: Drop mandatory write-test-first ordering in smith

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-09-01

## Context

`smith` (formerly `lambda`) mandated a strict TDD cycle for every task: write the failing test, confirm it fails (red), write the minimal implementation, confirm it passes (green), commit. `navigator`'s `planner` encoded this into `plan@1` itself — every task specified "a failing test written before any implementation code" and "expected failure output" as required fields, and rejected any task not in that order.

The rationale for this ordering was that the red phase is the only moment you know a test would actually fail if the code were wrong — without it, a test could be written after the fact to match whatever the implementation happened to do, producing coverage numbers rather than evidence.

A controlled comparison of TDD-in-the-agent-loop versus non-TDD agent workflows (Birgitta Böckeler, ThoughtWorks, published on martinfowler.com, "TDD inside the agent loop — theater or actual value?") found:

- Agent-written code showed no discernible quality difference between TDD and non-TDD workflows when blind-judged by another model — non-TDD solutions were ranked as good or slightly better in most batches.
- TDD workflows used 2.96x–8.50x more tokens across small/medium/large tasks, with no corresponding benefit.
- Mutation scores — a harder, more direct signal of whether a test suite would catch a wrong implementation than pass/fail alone — showed no meaningful difference between TDD and non-TDD runs. Regression-catching capability was equal either way.
- The mechanism: "the TDD instructions actively work against \[an] up front design step. The design in those runs emerged from the sum of many locally-minimal decisions and was rarely revisited, so it tended to land on whatever shape the first test happened to lock in." Non-TDD runs "created the full design (architectur<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="333" />tion, and the exact tests proving its criteria — order between the latter two is not mandated.

This does not touch `mutator`, `reviewer`, or `exit-gate` — every downstream check ("does the full suite pass," "did mutation testing run," "is every criterion proven") is unchanged. It also does not touch bug-repair workflows elsewhere in the ecosystem where reproducing a failure before fixing it remains the right practice (see `shared/agent-best-practices.md`'s "Repair" cognitive mode) — that case has a clear causal reason for the ordering (proving the bug is real) that doesn't apply to fresh feature implementation from a spec.

This updates the "repair" cognitive mode's characterization in `docs/adr/003-cognitive-mode-separation.md` ("minimum change + red-green verification") for `implementer` specifically — that ADR is left as historical record rather than rewritten; this decision supersedes it for `smith`'s fresh-implementation case, not for genuine bug-repair workflows where reproduce-then-fix still applies.

## Consequences

Lower token cost per task (the Böckeler comparison suggests several times lower, though this repo has not run its own controlled comparison). Implementation approach is decided before any test exists to lock it in prematurely. The safety net that previously came from "the test failed first" now comes entirely from mutation testing — if a target workspace's mutation tool is unavailable, `mutator` already records this as a coverage gap rather than a hard block (pre-existing behavior), which means test-quality assurance is weaker in that specific case than it would be under strict TDD's red-phase guarantee; this is an accepted tradeoff, not an oversight. This change is based on one practitioner's controlled comparison, not a study of this ecosystem's own agents — if evidence emerges that this repo's tasks behave differently, this decision should be revisited the same way it was made: by measuring, not by argument.

# Repository Constitution

Authoritative rules for all plugins in this repository. EARS-format hard constraints — the fence that all plugin development must stay inside. The interior (how an agent reasons, searches, and decides) is intentionally unconstrained.

All rules use EARS notation: WHEN / IF / WHERE / WHILE / THE SYSTEM SHALL.

---

## Plugin Structure

WHEN a new plugin is created, it SHALL conform to the directory layout:
```
plugins/<id>/
├── plugin.json
├── README.md
├── CHANGELOG.md
├── skills/<id>/SKILL.md
└── agents/*.md
```

A new plugin SHALL default to a single skill directory named after the plugin id. IF the plugin's scope grows to cover several genuinely independent, heterogeneous user intents on the same artifact (not a linear pipeline invoked as one flow), the plugin author MAY split `skills/<id>/` into multiple directories — `skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` per skill — each still conforming to the frontmatter and body rules below. The skill-routing key is the directory name, not the frontmatter `name:` field.

WHEN a plugin manifest (`plugin.json`) is authored, it SHALL include: `id`, `version` (semver), `description`, `skills`, and `agents` (list of file paths).

IF a plugin is superseded by another, it SHALL be deleted from the repository rather than marked deprecated.

---

## Agent Structure

WHEN an agent prompt is authored, it SHALL define five named sections in the body, in this order: `<constitution>`, `<backstory>`, `<goal>`, `<judgment>`, and `<output>`.

WHEN an agent body's `<constitution>` section is authored or amended, it SHALL be byte-for-byte identical across every agent file in the ecosystem — this is the shared static prefix the Static Prompt Prefix Invariant depends on; any per-character difference breaks prompt-cache matching for every agent, not just the one edited.

WHEN an agent uses a shared reference file during e<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="3552" />tmatter, it SHALL default to a single lifecycle-stage word.

IF a single word does not communicate what the skill acts on, the plugin author SHALL use a more specific multi-word name instead (e.g. `post-review`, not `post`).

Skill names SHALL NOT be prefixed with their own plugin id to resolve a collision with another plugin's skill name (e.g. `courier-post`) — the plugin-qualified invocation (`<plugin>:<skill>`) already disambiguates two plugins using the same bare skill name, so prefixing the name itself duplicates that and adds no clarity.

---

## Reference Files

WHEN language-specific reference files are authored, they SHALL be split by concern: hazards, smells, tooling — one file per concern per language.

WHEN the top-level language index file (`rust.md`, `typescript.md`) is referenced, it SHALL redirect to the appropriate split file rather than containing content directly.

---

## Documentation

WHEN a plugin is published, it SHALL include a `README.md` with: purpose, when-to-use trigger phrases, agent table with modes and tiers, pipeline diagram, output schema reference, and install instructions.

WHEN editing Markdown, THE SYSTEM SHALL keep each prose paragraph on one physical source line — Markdown prose SHALL NEVER be manually wrapped.

WHEN authoring Markdown, THE SYSTEM SHALL use a succinct, friendly, engineering-focused voice and favor scannable headings, lists, tables, diagrams, and charts over dense prose.

WHEN CONTRIBUTING.md is updated, it SHALL reflect the current authoring checklist — not the authoring conventions from a prior era.

## What Luu tested

Luu compared 26 testing and verification prompts plus four skills using a Rust Zstd implementation task. GPT-5.6 Sol ran at medium and xhigh effort, averaging 80 runs per condition. Success required passing 100% of hidden tests, with cost tracked alongside correctness. Similar qualitative results appeared on IMAP and other RFC tasks.

His central findings were:

- Naming a technique rarely makes agents use it competently.
- Agents often wrap ordinary unit tests in the requested framework.
- Tests concentrate on easy or invalid inputs rather than risky state.
- Formal methods prove irrelevant or vacuous properties.
- More tests, TDD, and iterative green runs can reinforce incorrect behavior.
- Large tutorial-like skills increase cost without improving correctness.
- The most promising custom skill identified likely mistakes, demanded discriminating asymmetric examples, encouraged structured inputs, and requested independent derivation—but even that was followed inconsistently.
- Default prompting performed surprisingly well because many added instructions induced low-value work.

Luu explicitly cautions against treating condition rankings as definitive because of variance and idiosyncratic failures. [Dan Luu’s complete methodology and analysis](https://danluu.com/agentic-testing/).

## Where Callisto did better

| Dimension | Better Callisto evidence |
|---|---|
| Architecture before patches | Codex repeatedly traced crate ownership, semantic models, durable release state, and producer/consumer boundaries before implementation. Release-PR policy moved from Bash into typed model and CLI decisions rather than accumulating shell patches. |
| Exact failure scenarios | Claude eventually added the original fixed-group cascade scenario, plus decision-tampering and manifest/decision-disagreement tests. These exercise semantic failures, not merely line coverage: [durable release tests](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-cli/tests/durable_release_e2e_tests.rs:252). |
| Meaningful mutation | A Claude/Lambda verification reportedly made eight deliberate mutations and found a missing cross-glob contamination assertion. That is genuine mutation reasoning, unlike the superficial “mutation testing” Luu commonly observed. |
| Iterative human steering | Prompts such as “Are we sure this is the only issue?”, “think holistically,” and “what did we miss?” materially improved the work. This agrees with Luu’s observation that inspecting the result and adding a few targeted instructions can outperform a fully front-loaded generic skill. |
| Independent checking | The primary Claude agent repeatedly inspected subagent diffs and reran tests after subagents stopped prematurely. It found a missed `--all-targets` Clippy issue and rejected completion summaries that were not supported by repository state. |
| Structural response | Once repeated defects were recognized, the work moved toward shared models, canonical helpers, architecture tests, and explicit sibling discipline instead of merely duplicating patches. |

## Where we failed just as much

The strongest counterexample is Codex’s PR #46.

It introduced a thoughtful typed release-PR model, black-box action tests, stale-state verification, and passed 1,265 tests. Production still broke because the tests stubbed the `callisto` binary with hand-written camelCase JSON. The real binary emitted snake_case enum fields, while the shell expected camelCase.

That is almost a textbook instance of Luu’s result: the agent’s tests passed because the oracle encoded the intended output rather than exercising the real producer-consumer boundary. Callisto now contains a real-binary contract test whose opening comment documents this exact structural blind spot: [binary contract test](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.github/actions/callisto-action/tests/test_release_pr_decide_binary_contract.sh:2).

Other repeated failures:

- PR #59 fixed a stale-member crash in the linked-group branch but left the structurally identical fixed-group branch unguarded a few lines away.
- Claude initially declared the serialization issue fixed; only after “Are we sure this is the only issue?” did it discover a sibling Serde case and the missing integration-test boundary.
- Codex introduced `rg` into a contract test deliberately executed with a restricted `PATH`. Local checks passed; CI caught the environmental assumption.
- Large passing-test counts were repeatedly reported as confidence signals even when the omitted test was the defining production scenario.
- Some subagents reported completion while their test runs were still pending. The parent’s later verification helped, but the workflow itself produced unreliable completion evidence.
- The newest Claude workflow used many parallel agents and hundreds of millions of cached tokens. That may improve recall, but it also resembles Luu’s warning that structured workflows can substantially increase work without demonstrated correctness gains.

There is no defensible winner from these sessions.

- Codex was particularly strong at architecture, semantic-model reconciliation, live PR-stack analysis, typed boundaries, and explicit authorization models.
- Codex’s main weakness was real-boundary verification: its sophisticated design still shipped a producer/consumer mismatch and a CI-environment assumption.
- Claude was stronger during post-incident recovery: it added exact regression scenarios, tamper tests, and eventually broad defect-pattern audits.
- Claude still needed user pressure to expand from an instance to its siblings, and one of its own fixes left the adjacent equivalent defect behind.

The task phase, accumulated repository knowledge, user steering, and plugin generation explain at least as much as the model identity.

The timeline matters:

- The August Codex work mostly used repository-local workflows and the older Bug Hunter setup, not today’s native Wisp plugin suite.
- Earlier Claude work used the pre-rename Lambda/Proof generation. It produced at least one good mutation result but remained TDD-heavy.
- Wisp 4.1 removed mandatory test-first ordering on September 1 after external controlled evidence showed higher cost without better quality. That aligns closely with Luu’s TDD result: [ADR-008](/Users/gabe/Projects/agent-plugins/docs/adr/008-drop-test-first-ordering.md).

The current design is substantially better targeted:

- Smith requires syntactic and semantic sibling evidence, including negative search evidence: [reviewer](/Users/gabe/Projects/agent-plugins/plugins/smith/agents/reviewer.md:45).
- Its gate blocks unresolved siblings and incomplete architecture routes: [exit gate](/Users/gabe/Projects/agent-plugins/plugins/smith/agents/exit-gate.md:58).

This is strong evidence that the plugins have learned from the failures. It is not evidence yet that agents reliably follow the new guidance.

## Remaining plugin risks

Two aspects still deserve adjustment or measurement:

- Smith’s fixed seven-step cycle and mandatory mutation pass after every batch may be too prescriptive. It is much smaller and more focused than the large tutorial skills Luu tested, but it could still add substantial cost where mutation provides little information.
- Mutation only evaluates implemented behavior. It cannot mutate missing states, omitted branches, absent sibling handling, or a producer-consumer test that was never written.

I would keep the hard outcome gates but make technique selection risk-driven:

- Require the agent to name the likely mistake and the check that distinguishes correct from incorrect behavior.
- For changed boundaries, require at least one test using the real producer through the real consumer—not hand-authored substitute output.
- Use actual mutation tooling for existing logic, plus deliberate semantic mutations for missing-state and boundary defects.
- For parsers, graphs, protocols, and formatters, prefer structured valid generators over random invalid input.
- Record why a chosen technique can expose the named fault class. Merely running the tool is insufficient.

5. Keep unsupervised runs separate from human-steered runs.

# ADR-008: Drop mandatory write-test-first ordering in smith

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-09-01

## Context

`smith` (formerly `lambda`) mandated a strict TDD cycle for every task: write the failing test, confirm it fails (red), write the minimal implementation, confirm it passes (green), commit. `navigator`'s `planner` encoded this into `plan@1` itself — every task specified "a failing test written before any implementation code" and "expected failure output" as required fields, and rejected any task not in that order.

The rationale for this ordering was that the red phase is the only moment you know a test would actually fail if the code were wrong — without it, a test could be written after the fact to match whatever the implementation happened to do, producing coverage numbers rather than evidence.

A controlled comparison of TDD-in-the-agent-loop versus non-TDD agent workflows (Birgitta Böckeler, ThoughtWorks, published on martinfowler.com, "TDD inside the agent loop — theater or actual value?") found:

- Agent-written code showed no discernible quality difference between TDD and non-TDD workflows when blind-judged by another model — non-TDD solutions were ranked as good or slightly better in most batches.
- TDD workflows used 2.96x–8.50x more tokens across small/medium/large tasks, with no corresponding benefit.
- Mutation scores — a harder, more direct signal of whether a test suite would catch a wrong implementation than pass/fail alone — showed no meaningful difference between TDD and non-TDD runs. Regression-catching capability was equal either way.
- The mechanism: "the TDD instructions actively work against \[an] up front design step. The design in those runs emerged from the sum of many locally-minimal decisions and was rarely revisited, so it tended to land on whatever shape the first test happened to lock in." Non-TDD runs "created the full design (architectur<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="333" />tion, and the exact tests proving its criteria — order between the latter two is not mandated.

This does not touch `mutator`, `reviewer`, or `exit-gate` — every downstream check ("does the full suite pass," "did mutation testing run," "is every criterion proven") is unchanged. It also does not touch bug-repair workflows elsewhere in the ecosystem where reproducing a failure before fixing it remains the right practice (see `shared/agent-best-practices.md`'s "Repair" cognitive mode) — that case has a clear causal reason for the ordering (proving the bug is real) that doesn't apply to fresh feature implementation from a spec.

This updates the "repair" cognitive mode's characterization in `docs/adr/003-cognitive-mode-separation.md` ("minimum change + red-green verification") for `implementer` specifically — that ADR is left as historical record rather than rewritten; this decision supersedes it for `smith`'s fresh-implementation case, not for genuine bug-repair workflows where reproduce-then-fix still applies.

## Consequences

Lower token cost per task (the Böckeler comparison suggests several times lower, though this repo has not run its own controlled comparison). Implementation approach is decided before any test exists to lock it in prematurely. The safety net that previously came from "the test failed first" now comes entirely from mutation testing — if a target workspace's mutation tool is unavailable, `mutator` already records this as a coverage gap rather than a hard block (pre-existing behavior), which means test-quality assurance is weaker in that specific case than it would be under strict TDD's red-phase guarantee; this is an accepted tradeoff, not an oversight. This change is based on one practitioner's controlled comparison, not a study of this ecosystem's own agents — if evidence emerges that this repo's tasks behave differently, this decision should be revisited the same way it was made: by measuring, not by argument.

Luu compared 26 testing and verification prompts plus four skills using a Rust Zstd implementation task. GPT-5.6 Sol ran at medium and xhigh effort, averaging 80 runs per condition. His central findings were:

- Naming a technique rarely makes agents use it competently.
- Agents often wrap ordinary unit tests in the requested framework.
- Tests concentrate on easy or invalid inputs rather than risky state.
- Formal methods prove irrelevant or vacuous properties.
- More tests, TDD, and iterative green runs can reinforce incorrect behavior.

# ADR-008: Drop mandatory write-test-first ordering in smith

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-09-01

## Context

`smith` (formerly `lambda`) mandated a strict TDD cycle for every task: write the failing test, confirm it fails (red), write the minimal implementation, confirm it passes (green), commit. `navigator`'s `planner` encoded this into `plan@1` itself — every task specified "a failing test written before any implementation code" and "expected failure output" as required fields, and rejected any task not in that order.

The rationale for this ordering was that the red phase is the only moment you know a test would actually fail if the code were wrong — without it, a test could be written after the fact to match whatever the implementation happened to do, producing coverage numbers rather than evidence.

A controlled comparison of TDD-in-the-agent-loop versus non-TDD agent workflows (Birgitta Böckeler, ThoughtWorks, published on martinfowler.com, "TDD inside the agent loop — theater or actual value?") found:

- Agent-written code showed no discernible quality difference between TDD and non-TDD workflows when blind-judged by another model — non-TDD solutions were ranked as good or slightly better in most batches.
- TDD workflows used 2.96x–8.50x more tokens across small/medium/large tasks, with no corresponding benefit.
- Mutation scores — a harder, more direct signal of whether a test suite would catch a wrong implementation than pass/fail alone — showed no meaningful difference between TDD and non-TDD runs. Regression-catching capability was equal either way.
- The mechanism: "the TDD instructions actively work against \[an] up front design step. The design in those runs emerged from the sum of many locally-minimal decisions and was rarely revisited, so it tended to land on whatever shape the first test happened to lock in." Non-TDD runs "created the full design (architectur<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="333" />tion, and the exact tests proving its criteria — order between the latter two is not mandated.

This does not touch `mutator`, `reviewer`, or `exit-gate` — every downstream check ("does the full suite pass," "did mutation testing run," "is every criterion proven") is unchanged. It also does not touch bug-repair workflows elsewhere in the ecosystem where reproducing a failure before fixing it remains the right practice (see `shared/agent-best-practices.md`'s "Repair" cognitive mode) — that case has a clear causal reason for the ordering (proving the bug is real) that doesn't apply to fresh feature implementation from a spec.

This updates the "repair" cognitive mode's characterization in `docs/adr/003-cognitive-mode-separation.md` ("minimum change + red-green verification") for `implementer` specifically — that ADR is left as historical record rather than rewritten; this decision supersedes it for `smith`'s fresh-implementation case, not for genuine bug-repair workflows where reproduce-then-fix still applies.

## Consequences

Lower token cost per task (the Böckeler comparison suggests several times lower, though this repo has not run its own controlled comparison). Implementation approach is decided before any test exists to lock it in prematurely. The safety net that previously came from "the test failed first" now comes entirely from mutation testing — if a target workspace's mutation tool is unavailable, `mutator` already records this as a coverage gap rather than a hard block (pre-existing behavior), which means test-quality assurance is weaker in that specific case than it would be under strict TDD's red-phase guarantee; this is an accepted tradeoff, not an oversight. This change is based on one practitioner's controlled comparison, not a study of this ecosystem's own agents — if evidence emerges that this repo's tasks behave differently, this decision should be revisited the same way it was made: by measuring, not by argument.

# Repository Constitution

Authoritative rules for all plugins in this repository. EARS-format hard constraints — the fence that all plugin development must stay inside. The interior (how an agent reasons, searches, and decides) is intentionally unconstrained.

All rules use EARS notation: WHEN / IF / WHERE / WHILE / THE SYSTEM SHALL.

---

## Plugin Structure

WHEN a new plugin is created, it SHALL conform to the directory layout:
```
plugins/<id>/
├── plugin.json
├── README.md
├── CHANGELOG.md
├── skills/<id>/SKILL.md
└── agents/*.md
```

A new plugin SHALL default to a single skill directory named after the plugin id. IF the plugin's scope grows to cover several genuinely independent, heterogeneous user intents on the same artifact (not a linear pipeline invoked as one flow), the plugin author MAY split `skills/<id>/` into multiple directories — `skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` per skill — each still conforming to the frontmatter and body rules below. The skill-routing key is the directory name, not the frontmatter `name:` field.

WHEN a plugin manifest (`plugin.json`) is authored, it SHALL include: `id`, `version` (semver), `description`, `skills`, and `agents` (list of file paths).

IF a plugin is superseded by another, it SHALL be deleted from the repository rather than marked deprecated.

---

## Agent Structure

WHEN an agent prompt is authored, it SHALL define five named sections in the body, in this order: `<constitution>`, `<backstory>`, `<goal>`, `<judgment>`, and `<output>`.

WHEN an agent body's `<constitution>` section is authored or amended, it SHALL be byte-for-byte identical across every agent file in the ecosystem — this is the shared static prefix the Static Prompt Prefix Invariant depends on; any per-character difference breaks prompt-cache matching for every agent, not just the one edited.

WHEN an agent uses a shared reference file during e<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="3552" />tmatter, it SHALL default to a single lifecycle-stage word.

IF a single word does not communicate what the skill acts on, the plugin author SHALL use a more specific multi-word name instead (e.g. `post-review`, not `post`).

Skill names SHALL NOT be prefixed with their own plugin id to resolve a collision with another plugin's skill name (e.g. `courier-post`) — the plugin-qualified invocation (`<plugin>:<skill>`) already disambiguates two plugins using the same bare skill name, so prefixing the name itself duplicates that and adds no clarity.

---

## Reference Files

WHEN language-specific reference files are authored, they SHALL be split by concern: hazards, smells, tooling — one file per concern per language.

WHEN the top-level language index file (`rust.md`, `typescript.md`) is referenced, it SHALL redirect to the appropriate split file rather than containing content directly.

---

## Documentation

WHEN a plugin is published, it SHALL include a `README.md` with: purpose, when-to-use trigger phrases, agent table with modes and tiers, pipeline diagram, output schema reference, and install instructions.

WHEN editing Markdown, THE SYSTEM SHALL keep each prose paragraph on one physical source line — Markdown prose SHALL NEVER be manually wrapped.

WHEN authoring Markdown, THE SYSTEM SHALL use a succinct, friendly, engineering-focused voice and favor scannable headings, lists, tables, diagrams, and charts over dense prose.

WHEN CONTRIBUTING.md is updated, it SHALL reflect the current authoring checklist — not the authoring conventions from a prior era.

WHEN a new agent-authoring convention is added to this constitution or to CONTRIBUTING.md's checklist — a new required section, a new required check — THE SYSTEM SHALL update `mason:scaffolder` and `mason:auditor` in the same change. A convention `mason` cannot generate or verify is documented, not enforced, and every plugin scaffolded before the update inherits the gap silently.

## What Luu tested

Luu compared 26 testing and verification prompts plus four skills using a Rust Zstd implementation task. GPT-5.6 Sol ran at medium and xhigh effort, averaging 80 runs per condition. Success required passing 100% of hidden tests, with cost tracked alongside correctness. Similar qualitative results appeared on IMAP and other RFC tasks.

His central findings were:

- Naming a technique rarely makes agents use it competently.
- Agents often wrap ordinary unit tests in the requested framework.
- Tests concentrate on easy or invalid inputs rather than risky state.
- Formal methods prove irrelevant or vacuous properties.
- More tests, TDD, and iterative green runs can reinforce incorrect behavior.
- Large tutorial-like skills increase cost without improving correctness.
- The most promising custom skill identified likely mistakes, demanded discriminating asymmetric examples, encouraged structured inputs, and requested independent derivation—but even that was followed inconsistently.
- Default prompting performed surprisingly well because many added instructions induced low-value work.

Luu explicitly cautions against treating condition rankings as definitive because of variance and idiosyncratic failures. [Dan Luu’s complete methodology and analysis](https://danluu.com/agentic-testing/).

## Where Callisto did better

| Dimension | Better Callisto evidence |
|---|---|
| Architecture before patches | Codex repeatedly traced crate ownership, semantic models, durable release state, and producer/consumer boundaries before implementation. Release-PR policy moved from Bash into typed model and CLI decisions rather than accumulating shell patches. |

| Meaningful mutation | A Claude/Lambda verification reportedly made eight deliberate mutations and found a missing cross-glob contamination assertion. That is genuine mutation reasoning, unlike the superficial “mutation testing” Luu commonly observed. |
| Iterative human steering | Prompts such as “Are we sure this is the only issue?”, “think holistically,” and “what did we miss?” materially improved the work. This agrees with Luu’s observation that inspecting the result and adding a few targeted instructions can outperform a fully front-loaded generic skill. |
| Independent checking | The primary Claude agent repeatedly inspected subagent diffs and reran tests after subagents stopped prematurely. It found a missed `--all-targets` Clippy issue and rejected completion summaries that were not supported by repository state. |
| Structural response | Once repeated defects were recognized, the work moved toward shared models, canonical helpers, architecture tests, and explicit sibling discipline instead of merely duplicating patches. |

## Where we failed just as much

The strongest counterexample is Codex’s PR #46.

It introduced a thoughtful typed release-PR model, black-box action tests, stale-state verification, and passed 1,265 tests. Production still broke because the tests stubbed the `callisto` binary with hand-written camelCase JSON. The real binary emitted snake_case enum fields, while the shell expected camelCase.

That is almost a textbook instance of Luu’s result: the agent’s tests passed because the oracle encoded the intended output rather than exercising the real producer-consumer boundary. Callisto now contains a real-binary contract test whose opening comment documents this exact structural blind spot: [binary contract test](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.github/actions/callisto-action/tests/test_release_pr_decide_binary_contract.sh:2).

- PR #59 fixed a stale-member crash in the linked-group branch but left the structurally identical fixed-group branch unguarded a few lines away.
- Claude initially declared the serialization issue fixed; only after “Are we sure this is the only issue?” did it discover a sibling Serde case and the missing integration-test boundary.
- Codex introduced `rg` into a contract test deliberately executed with a restricted `PATH`. Local checks passed; CI caught the environmental assumption.
- Large passing-test counts were repeatedly reported as confidence signals even when the omitted test was the defining production scenario.
- Some subagents reported completion while their test runs were still pending. The parent’s later verification helped, but the workflow itself produced unreliable completion evidence.
- The newest Claude workflow used many parallel agents and hundreds of millions of cached tokens. That may improve recall, but it also resembles Luu’s warning that structured workflows can substantially increase work without demonstrated correctness gains.

There is no defensible winner from these sessions.

- Codex was particularly strong at architecture, semantic-model reconciliation, live PR-stack analysis, typed boundaries, and explicit authorization models.
- Codex’s main weakness was real-boundary verification: its sophisticated design still shipped a producer/consumer mismatch and a CI-environment assumption.
- Claude was stronger during post-incident recovery: it added exact regression scenarios, tamper tests, and eventually broad defect-pattern audits.

Two aspects still deserve adjustment or measurement:

Luu compared 26 testing and verification prompts plus four skills using a Rust Zstd implementation task. GPT-5.6 Sol ran at medium and xhigh effort, averaging 80 runs per condition. Success required passing 100% of hidden tests, with cost tracked alongside correctness. Similar qualitative results appeared on IMAP and other RFC tasks.

His central findings were:

- Naming a technique rarely makes agents use it competently.
- Agents often wrap ordinary unit tests in the requested framework.
- Tests concentrate on easy or invalid inputs rather than risky state.
- Formal methods prove irrelevant or vacuous properties.
- More tests, TDD, and iterative green runs can reinforce incorrect behavior.
- Large tutorial-like skills increase cost without improving correctness.
- The most promising custom skill identified likely mistakes, demanded discriminating asymmetric examples, encouraged structured inputs, and requested independent derivation—but even that was followed inconsistently.
- Default prompting performed surprisingly well because many added instructions induced low-value work.

Luu explicitly cautions against treating condition rankings as definitive because of variance and idiosyncratic failures. [Dan Luu’s complete methodology and analysis](https://danluu.com/agentic-testing/).

## Where Callisto did better

| Dimension | Better Callisto evidence |
|---|---|
| Architecture before patches | Codex repeatedly traced crate ownership, semantic models, durable release state, and producer/consumer boundaries before implementation. Release-PR policy moved from Bash into typed model and CLI decisions rather than accumulating shell patches. |
| Exact failure scenarios | Claude eventually added the original fixed-group cascade scenario, plus decision-tampering and manifest/decision-disagreement tests. These exercise semantic failures, not merely line coverage: [durable release tests](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-cli/tests/durable_release_e2e_tests.rs:252). |
| Meaningful mutation | A Claude/Lambda verification reportedly made eight deliberate mutations and found a missing cross-glob contamination assertion. That is genuine mutation reasoning, unlike the superficial “mutation testing” Luu commonly observed. |
| Iterative human steering | Prompts such as “Are we sure this is the only issue?”, “think holistically,” and “what did we miss?” materially improved the work. This agrees with Luu’s observation that inspecting the result and adding a few targeted instructions can outperform a fully front-loaded generic skill. |
| Independent checking | The primary Claude agent repeatedly inspected subagent diffs and reran tests after subagents stopped prematurely. It found a missed `--all-targets` Clippy issue and rejected completion summaries that were not supported by repository state. |
| Structural response | Once repeated defects were recognized, the work moved toward shared models, canonical helpers, architecture tests, and explicit sibling discipline instead of merely duplicating patches. |

The strongest counterexample is Codex’s PR #46.

It introduced a thoughtful typed release-PR model, black-box action tests, stale-state verification, and passed 1,265 tests. Production still broke because the tests stubbed the `callisto` binary with hand-written camelCase JSON. The real binary emitted snake_case enum fields, while the shell expected camelCase.

That is almost a textbook instance of Luu’s result: the agent’s tests passed because the oracle encoded the intended output rather than exercising the real producer-consumer boundary. Callisto now contains a real-binary contract test whose opening comment documents this exact structural blind spot: [binary contract test](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.github/actions/callisto-action/tests/test_release_pr_decide_binary_contract.sh:2).

- Codex introduced `rg` into a contract test deliberately executed with a restricted `PATH`. Local checks passed; CI caught the environmental assumption.
- Large passing-test counts were repeatedly reported as confidence signals even when the omitted test was the defining production scenario.
- Some subagents reported completion while their test runs were still pending. The parent’s later verification helped, but the workflow itself produced unreliable completion evidence.
- The newest Claude workflow used many parallel agents and hundreds of millions of cached tokens. That may improve recall, but it also resembles Luu’s warning that structured workflows can substantially increase work without demonstrated correctness gains.

There is no defensible winner from these sessions.

- Codex was particularly strong at architecture, semantic-model reconciliation, live PR-stack analysis, typed boundaries, and explicit authorization models.
- Codex’s main weakness was real-boundary verification: its sophisticated design still shipped a producer/consumer mismatch and a CI-environment assumption.
- Claude was stronger during post-incident recovery: it added exact regression scenarios, tamper tests, and eventually broad defect-pattern audits.
- Claude still needed user pressure to expand from an instance to its siblings, and one of its own fixes left the adjacent equivalent defect behind.

The task phase, accumulated repository knowledge, user steering, and plugin generation explain at least as much as the model identity.

The timeline matters:

- The August Codex work mostly used repository-local workflows and the older Bug Hunter setup, not today’s native Wisp plugin suite.

## Remaining plugin risks

Two aspects still deserve adjustment or measurement:

- Smith’s fixed seven-step cycle and mandatory mutation pass after every batch may be too prescriptive. It is much smaller and more focused than the large tutorial skills Luu tested, but it could still add substantial cost where mutation provides little information.
- Mutation only evaluates implemented behavior. It cannot mutate missing states, omitted branches, absent sibling handling, or a producer-consumer test that was never written.

I would keep the hard outcome gates but make technique selection risk-driven:

- Require the agent to name the likely mistake and the check that distinguishes correct from incorrect behavior.
- For changed boundaries, require at least one test using the real producer through the real consumer—not hand-authored substitute output.
- Use actual mutation tooling for existing logic, plus deliberate semantic mutations for missing-state and boundary defects.
- For parsers, graphs, protocols, and formatters, prefer structured valid generators over random invalid input.
- Record why a chosen technique can expose the named fault class. Merely running the tool is insufficient.

Extend the existing [behavioral-evaluation protocol](/Users/gabe/Projects/agent-plugins/docs/codex-behavioral-evaluation.md:32) with a Callisto defect corpus:

1. Create clean pre-fix snapshots for the Serde casing, fixed/linked sibling, empty pathspec, `Ord`/`Eq`, restricted-PATH, and cascade-release defects.
2. Run identical prompts under:

   - the historically available plugin version;
   - Wisp 4.3;

3. Hide tests for:

   - its syntactic sibling;
   - its semantic sibling;
   - the real producer-consumer boundary;
   - an environment variant;
   - the architectural recurrence condition.
4. Record full hidden-suite pass rate, sibling recall, oracle independence, actual technique use, cost, latency, and whether the skill was opened.
5. Keep unsupervised runs separate from human-steered runs.
6. Start with 20 runs per condition as a pilot; use 50–80 before drawing comparative conclusions.

The existing schema records harness, host, model, and roles, but not plugin version, condition, cost, technique compliance, or hidden-test results: [harness-evaluation schema](/Users/gabe/Projects/agent-plugins/shared/schemas/harness-evaluation@1.json:16). Callisto’s sessions show better testing behavior than the typical runs Dan Luu observed—but we still reproduced several of his most important failure modes.

The improvement is real but not yet attributable to the plugins with confidence. The newest Wisp 4.3 guidance directly addresses the failures found in Callisto, but it was released after the latest reviewed Claude session ended. We have design evidence, not post-release performance evidence.

## What Luu tested

Luu compared 26 testing and verification prompts plus four skills using a Rust Zstd implementation task. GPT-5.6 Sol ran at medium and xhigh effort, averaging 80 runs per condition. Success required passing 100% of hidden tests, with cost tracked alongside correctness. Similar qualitative results appeared on IMAP and other RFC tasks.

His central findings were:

- Naming a technique rarely makes agents use it competently.
- Agents often wrap ordinary unit tests in the requested framework.
- Tests concentrate on easy or invalid inputs rather than risky state.
- Formal methods prove irrelevant or vacuous properties.
- More tests, TDD, and iterative green runs can reinforce incorrect behavior.
- Large tutorial-like skills increase cost without improving correctness.
- The most promising custom skill identified likely mistakes, demanded discriminating asymmetric examples, encouraged structured inputs, and requested independent derivation—but even that was followed inconsistently.
- Default prompting performed surprisingly well because many added instructions induced low-value work.

Luu explicitly cautions against treating condition rankings as definitive because of variance and idiosyncratic failures. [Dan Luu’s complete methodology and analysis](https://danluu.com/agentic-testing/).

## Where Callisto did better

| Dimension | Better Callisto evidence |
|---|---|
| Architecture before patches | Codex repeatedly traced crate ownership, semantic models, durable release state, and producer/consumer boundaries before implementation. Release-PR policy moved from Bash into typed model and CLI decisions rather than accumulating shell patches. |
| Exact failure scenarios | Claude eventually added the original fixed-group cascade scenario, plus decision-tampering and manifest/decision-disagreement tests. These exercise semantic failures, not merely line coverage: [durable release tests](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-cli/tests/durable_release_e2e_tests.rs:252). |
| Meaningful mutation | A Claude/Lambda verification reportedly made eight deliberate mutations and found a missing cross-glob contamination assertion. That is genuine mutation reasoning, unlike the superficial “mutation testing” Luu commonly observed. |
| Iterative human steering | Prompts such as “Are we sure this is the only issue?”, “think holistically,” and “what did we miss?” materially improved the work. This agrees with Luu’s observation that inspecting the result and adding a few targeted instructions can outperform a fully front-loaded generic skill. |
| Independent checking | The primary Claude agent repeatedly inspected subagent diffs and reran tests after subagents stopped prematurely. It found a missed `--all-targets` Clippy issue and rejected completion summaries that were not supported by repository state. |
| Structural response | Once repeated defects were recognized, the work moved toward shared models, canonical helpers, architecture tests, and explicit sibling discipline instead of merely duplicating patches. |

## Where we failed just as much

The strongest counterexample is Codex’s PR #46.

It introduced a thoughtful typed release-PR model, black-box action tests, stale-state verification, and passed 1,265 tests. Production still broke because the tests stubbed the `callisto` binary with hand-written camelCase JSON. The real binary emitted snake_case enum fields, while the shell expected camelCase.

That is almost a textbook instance of Luu’s result: the agent’s tests passed because the oracle encoded the intended output rather than exercising the real producer-consumer boundary. Callisto now contains a real-binary contract test whose opening comment documents this exact structural blind spot: [binary contract test](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.github/actions/callisto-action/tests/test_release_pr_decide_binary_contract.sh:2).

- PR #59 fixed a stale-member crash in the linked-group branch but left the structurally identical fixed-group branch unguarded a few lines away.
- Claude initially declared the serialization issue fixed; only after “Are we sure this is the only issue?” did it discover a sibling Serde case and the missing integration-test boundary.

- Large passing-test counts were repeatedly reported as confidence signals even when the omitted test was the defining production scenario.
- Some subagents reported completion while their test runs were still pending. The parent’s later verification helped, but the workflow itself produced unreliable completion evidence.
- The newest Claude workflow used many parallel agents and hundreds of millions of cached tokens. That may improve recall, but it also resembles Luu’s warning that structured workflows can substantially increase work without demonstrated correctness gains.

There is no defensible winner from these sessions.

- Codex was particularly strong at architecture, semantic-model reconciliation, live PR-stack analysis, typed boundaries, and explicit authorization models.

- Claude was stronger during post-incident recovery: it added exact regression scenarios, tamper tests, and eventually broad defect-pattern audits.

[52] assistant: ## Bottom line

Callisto’s sessions show better testing behavior than the typical runs Dan Luu observed—but we still reproduced several of his most important failure modes.

The improvement is real but not yet attributable to the plugins with confidence. The newest Wisp 4.3 guidance directly addresses the failures found in Callisto, but it was released after the latest reviewed Claude session ended. We have design evidence, not post-release performance evidence.

## What Luu tested

Luu compared 26 testing and verification prompts plus four skills using a Rust Zstd implementation task. GPT-5.6 Sol ran at medium and xhigh effort, averaging 80 runs per condition. Success required passing 100% of hidden tests, with cost tracked alongside correctness. Similar qualitative results appeared on IMAP and other RFC tasks.

His central findings were:

- Naming a technique rarely makes agents use it competently.
- Agents often wrap ordinary unit tests in the requested framework.
- Tests concentrate on easy or invalid inputs rather than risky state.
- Formal methods prove irrelevant or vacuous properties.
- More tests, TDD, and iterative green runs can reinforce incorrect behavior.
- Large tutorial-like skills increase cost without improving correctness.
- The most promising custom skill identified likely mistakes, demanded discriminating asymmetric examples, encouraged structured inputs, and requested independent derivation—but even that was followed inconsistently.
- Default prompting performed surprisingly well because many added instructions induced low-value work.

Luu explicitly cautions against treating condition rankings as definitive because of variance and idiosyncratic failures. [Dan Luu’s complete methodology and analysis](https://danluu.com/agentic-testing/).

## Where Callisto did better

| Dimension | Better Callisto evidence |
|---|---|
| Architecture before patches | Codex repeatedly traced crate ownership, semantic models, durable release state, and producer/consumer boundaries before implementation. Release-PR policy moved from Bash into typed model and CLI decisions rather than accumulating shell patches. |
| Exact failure scenarios | Claude eventually added the original fixed-group cascade scenario, plus decision-tampering and manifest/decision-disagreement tests. These exercise semantic failures, not merely line coverage: [durable release tests](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-cli/tests/durable_release_e2e_tests.rs:252). |
| Meaningful mutation | A Claude/Lambda verification reportedly made eight deliberate mutations and found a missing cross-glob contamination assertion. That is genuine mutation reasoning, unlike the superficial “mutation testing” Luu commonly observed. |
| Iterative human steering | Prompts such as “Are we sure this is the only issue?”, “think holistically,” and “what did we miss?” materially improved the work. This agrees with Luu’s observation that inspecting the result and adding a few targeted instructions can outperform a fully front-loaded generic skill. |
| Independent checking | The primary Claude agent repeatedly inspected subagent diffs and reran tests after subagents stopped prematurely. It found a missed `--all-targets` Clippy issue and rejected completion summaries that were not supported by repository state. |
| Structural response | Once repeated defects were recognized, the work moved toward shared models, canonical helpers, architecture tests, and explicit sibling discipline instead of merely duplicating patches. |

## Where we failed just as much

The strongest counterexample is Codex’s PR #46.

It introduced a thoughtful typed release-PR model, black-box action tests, stale-state verification, and passed 1,265 tests. Production still broke because the tests stubbed the `callisto` binary with hand-written camelCase JSON. The real binary emitted snake_case enum fields, while the shell expected camelCase.

That is almost a textbook instance of Luu’s result: the agent’s tests passed because the oracle encoded the intended output rather than exercising the real producer-consumer boundary. Callisto now contains a real-binary contract test whose opening comment documents this exact structural blind spot: [binary contract test](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.github/actions/callisto-action/tests/test_release_pr_decide_binary_contract.sh:2).

Other repeated failures:

- PR #59 fixed a stale-member crash in the linked-group branch but left the structurally identical fixed-group branch unguarded a few lines away.
- Claude initially declared the serialization issue fixed; only after “Are we sure this is the only issue?” did it discover a sibling Serde case and the missing integration-test boundary.
- Codex introduced `rg` into a contract test deliberately executed with a restricted `PATH`. Local checks passed; CI caught the environmental assumption.
- Large passing-test counts were repeatedly reported as confidence signals even when the omitted test was the defining production scenario.
- Some subagents reported completion while their test runs were still pending. The parent’s later verification helped, but the workflow itself produced unreliable completion evidence.
- The newest Claude workflow used many parallel agents and hundreds of millions of cached tokens. That may improve recall, but it also resembles Luu’s warning that structured workflows can substantially increase work without demonstrated correctness gains.

## Codex versus Claude

There is no defensible winner from these sessions.

- Codex was particularly strong at architecture, semantic-model reconciliation, live PR-stack analysis, typed boundaries, and explicit authorization models.
- Codex’s main weakness was real-boundary verification: its sophisticated design still shipped a producer/consumer mismatch and a CI-environment assumption.
- Claude was stronger during post-incident recovery: it added exact regression scenarios, tamper tests, and eventually broad defect-pattern audits.
- Claude still needed user pressure to expand from an instance to its siblings, and one of its own fixes left the adjacent equivalent defect behind.

The task phase, accumulated repository knowledge, user steering, and plugin generation explain at least as much as the model identity.

## Improvement over time

The timeline matters:

- The August Codex work mostly used repository-local workflows and the older Bug Hunter setup, not today’s native Wisp plugin suite.
- Earlier Claude work used the pre-rename Lambda/Proof generation. It produced at least one good mutation result but remained TDD-heavy.
- Wisp 4.1 removed mandatory test-first ordering on September 1 after external controlled evidence showed higher cost without better quality. That aligns closely with Luu’s TDD result: [ADR-008](/Users/gabe/Projects/agent-plugins/docs/adr/008-drop-test-first-ordering.md).
